list.listitem: Suspect lactose intolerance (LI) if symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating, and/or flatulence occur after the ingestion of lactose or lactose-containing products. C
The diagnosis of LI can be confirmed by hydrogen breath analysis and/or C/T-13910 genotyping, although clinical diagnosis and an empiric trial of therapy are usually sufficient. C
Individualize a lactose-free diet (see and ) to avoid symptoms and maintain adequate calcium intake. C
Probiotic supplementation may improve symptoms. SORT B
Lactaid caplets or chewable tablets, lactase drops and lactose-free milk are available and may be useful, but evidence is not supportive. C

background.definition: Lactose intolerance (LI) is a clinical syndrome of one or more of the following: abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, flatulence, and/or bloating after the ingestion of lactose or lactose-containing food substances. Presence and severity of symptoms varies based on the amount of lactose consumed, the degree of lactase deficiency, and the form of food substance in which the lactose is ingested.

list.listitem: Primary lactase deficiency affects 70% to 75% of the world's population. The highest prevalence is in Africa, Asia, and South America.
The prevalence of LI in North America is 79% of Native Americans, 51% of Hispanics, 21% of Caucasians, and 75% in African descendants.
The prevalence of primary LI in children aged 1-5 years is between 0% and 17.9% and the prevalence of secondary LI between 0% and 19%, based on a systematic review of the few studies available.

Authors of a systematic review found a global prevalence estimate of lactose malabsorption of 68% (95% CI 64-72), with a range of 28% (19-37) in western, southern, and northern Europe to 70% (57-83) in the Middle East. Prevalence rates varied based on the diagnostic approach, ranging from 74% (69-80) when genotyping data were used to 55% (46-65) using lactose tolerance test data and 57% (46-67) using hydrogen breath test data.

In a Swedish population registries study of 22,788 individuals with lactose intolerance, characterized by low milk and dairy product consumption, risks were decreased for cancers of the lung (SIR = 0.55), breast (SIR = 0.79), and ovaries (SIR = 0.61).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 case-control studies found a significantly lower bone density Z-score at most measured sites among post-menopausal women with primary LI compared to lactose absorbers although there was no overall difference in bone mineral density between groups.

Primary lactase deficiency is a progressive decline in lactase activity over time. Lactase activity is normally high at birth and progressively declines with aging, also known as lactase non-persistence. This is the most common cause of LI.
Secondary lactase deficiency is caused by damage to the small bowel (e.g., celiac disease, Crohn’s disease, infection, surgery) and subsequent loss of enzyme activity.
Congenital lactase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by complete absence of lactase activity that manifests at birth.

The gene for lactase-phlorizin hydrolase (LCT) is on chromosome 2(2q21), but a single-nucleotide mutation of cytosine to thymine, C/T-13910, is the locus involved in the regulation of the LCT activity. The CC genotype correlates 100% with low lactase activity (<10 mcg/g) on intestinal biopsy. TT individuals are lactase persistent (>10 mcg/g), and CT intermediate.

LCT diminishes from infancy to adulthood in an inconsistent fashion and at variable ages, based on race and ethnicity, to approximately 10% of its original levels in two-thirds to three-quarters of adults.
Lactose (a disaccharhide) is normally hydrolyzed by lactase into the monosaccharides glucose and galactose, which are absorbed into the blood stream.

Without lactase, as in LI, lactose can't be absorbed in the small intestine, so it is transported to the large intestine where it can't be absorbed in its disaccharide form. Instead, it is fermented by colonic bacteria, creating an osmotic load in the lumen and producing lactic acid, short chain fatty acids, and gases such as hydrogen. The excessive gas production causes luminal distention, leading to the symptoms abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea, flatulence, and/or bloating.
Symptoms vary and can include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, flatulence, or nausea. C
Diagnosis is most often clinical. Additional diagnostic testing may not be necessary if a lactose-free diet improves symptoms. C
If the diagnosis remains in doubt or confirmation is required, test by hydrogen breath analysis and/or C/T-13910 genotyping. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Young infants; allergic reaction presents with hives or wheezing, resolves
Pain relieved by stooling, mucus in stools, and incomplete evacuation sensation
Fever, weight loss, bloody diarrhea, and anemia
Nausea, vomiting, cysts or trophozoites in feces
Gluten sensitivity, weight loss, steatorrhea, and anemia
Upper abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, and vomiting
Burning abdominal pain that radiates to the back, hematemesis, and melena
Diarrhea, abdominal pain, flatulence, but no bleeding or systemic symptoms and normal gross appearance to colon

list.listitem: GI symptoms typically occur 0.5 to 3 hours after ingestion of lactose-containing products. As the degree of lactase deficiency varies among individuals, so does the amount of lactose required to produce symptoms.

Symptoms vary and can include abdominal pain, bloating, diarrhea, borborygmi, or nausea. The negative predictive value for bloating is 82% and the positive predictive value for diarrhea is 66%. A positive lactose hydrogen breath test was found in 21% of patients with 1 symptom, 40% with 2, 44% with 3, 67% with 4, and 82% with 5 symptoms.
Red flags, including bloody diarrhea, weight loss, fever, loss of appetite, and signs of obstruction or perforation, warrant further evaluation.

Symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and LI can be indistinguishable, and carbohydrate malabsorption is common in patients with IBS. In one study, 24.3% of IBS patients were shown to have isolated lactose malabsorption, and responded with symptomatic improvement after dietary restrictions. Consider testing for LI in patients with IBS.
Physical examination findings are nonspecific.
Diagnostic tests may not be necessary if patients' symptoms improve with dietary restrictions.

Genetic testing is the definitive test for LI. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) genotyping for C/T-13910 in symptomatic patients is a sensitive and specific test for LI. Symptomatic patients can first be genotyped. The CC genotype correlates 100% with positive hydrogen breath tests and requires no further testing. Individuals with the CT and TT genotypes should proceed to hydrogen breath testing.

Hydrogen breath analysis has been the preferred initial test for adult and pediatric patients. It is the most reliable indirect measure, is least invasive, and has a low cost. A hand-held chemical sensor gastrolyzer measures the exhaled hydrogen produced from the fermentation of unabsorbed lactose. A fasting patient consumes a standardized dose of lactose, and serial measurements of hydrogen excretion are taken for 3 hours of hydrogen excretion are taken. A value of 20 ppm above baseline is positive. Choosing the lower cutoff value of 10 ppm for probable LI increases the sensitivity (to 93.3%).

The lactose tolerance test, an absorption test, measures serial blood glucose levels after a lactose dose. A failure to increase at least 20 mg/dL (1.1 mmol/L) from baseline indicates LI. Sensitivity was 87% and specificity was 93%.

In a meta-analysis of trials of lactose breath hydrogen and lactose tolerance tests, both tests had relatively high sensitivity and specificity (overall sensitivity for the breath test was 0.88 [95% CI 0.85-0.90], specificity was 0.85 [95% CI 0.82-0.87]; overall sensitivity of the lactose tolerance test was 0.94 [95% CI 0.9-0.97], specificity was 0.90 [95% CI 0.84-0.95]).

The Gaxilose test is another noninvasive test that measures urinary xylose following oral administration of 4-galactosil-xilose; low levels of xylose are related to low lactase activity. In one study, sensitivity was 0.82 (95% CI 0.55-1) and specificity was 0.68 (95% CI 0.45-0.92).

A point-of-care test, the Biohit Lactose Intolerance Quick Test (LQT), is available. One study found that it had high sensitivity (100%) and moderate specificity (80%-86%) compared with biochemical disaccharides assay for diagnosing LI; this may be useful in ruling out LI when negative.
Fecal pH decreases due to the formation of fatty acids from the carbohydrate malabsorption. This test is infrequently used due to the high rate of false positives and false negatives.
A duodenal intestinal biopsy can directly measure the lactase levels. Symptoms may not correlate with levels.

In an Israeli study of both the lactose breath test and the LQT for 69 patients with suspected LI, the breath test was positive for lactose malabsorption in 32 patients (46%) and the LQT was positive for hypolactasia in 55 patients (80%); in one case, the LBT was positive and the LIQT was negative.

Among 46 children with LI of whom 64.4% were homozygous CC, the genetic test had better concordance with the breath test (k = 0.675) than the LQT (k = 0.301); none of the patients with normal LQT had lactose malabsorption.

In a study comparing symptoms score, a gaxilose test and lactose tolerance test using genetic testing as the gold standard, the highest degree of agreement with genetic testing (11 of 30 were confirmed with C/T-13910 polymorphism) was presence of diarrhea and symptom score after a 50 g lactose load along with the tolerance test (K > 0.60).
Suspect LI in patients with abdominal symptoms of pain, nausea, bloating, diarrhea, flatulence, or borborygmi occurring 0.5 to 3 hours after ingestion of dairy products.
Initial management is a lactose-free diet; be aware of hidden sources of lactose in the diet (). Resolution of symptoms with a lactose-free diet is often sufficient for diagnosis.
If the diagnosis is in doubt or confirmation is desired, test by hydrogen breath analysis and/or genetic testing. The combination can assist in differentiating between primary and secondary LI.

Consider other diagnoses and appropriate workup in patients presenting at age older than 40 years or who have bloody diarrhea, weight loss, signs of obstruction or perforation, loss of appetite, severe pain, fever, or other concerning symptoms.
Individualize the lactose-free diet (see ) to balance the amount of lactose ingestion and symptom avoidance. C
Dietary guidance and supplementation may be important to ensure adequate calcium. C
Lactaid caplets or chewable tablets are located in the pharmacy and may be taken each time dairy is ingested.
Lactaid milk, found in the grocery, comes in fat-free, low-fat, reduced fat, whole, calcium-fortified, and chocolate forms. All such milk is 100% lactose free.
Dairy ease milk is 100% lactose free and can be found in the grocery store. It comes in whole, 2%, and fat-free versions.

Lactase drops are available. Five drops per quart of milk reduces the lactose content by 70% to 80% and 10 drops by about 90%. Add drops to liquid milk or soft dairy products. Refrigerate for 24 hours before use.
A small study of 19 adults found that loperamide 8 mg has some benefit, but the cost and adverse effects limit its usefulness.

A small nonrandomized study found a possible benefit to the enteric antibiotic rifaximin. It is possible, however, that these patients were symptomatic from small intestine bacterial overgrowth, a condition with similar symptomatology and a positive hydrogen breath test, often mistaken for IBS and for which rifaximin is somewhat effective.

Though previous data have been mixed, a 2021 systematic review of 9 RCTs concluded that probiotic supplementation is beneficial by decreasing symptoms of abdominal cramping, diarrhea, vomiting, bloating, and flatulance.

After a 12-week lactose-free diet (), symptoms typically decrease significantly. In a small case series of 17 children with chronic abdominal pain and lactose-intolerance, most (94%) improved after 5 months but only 11 children (61%) were improved after 15 months of a lactose-restricted diet.
Individualize diet to balance dairy amount with tolerable symptoms. Most patients with lactose intolerance can tolerate 4 to 8 oz (approximately 1 cup) of milk taken with food.

Experiment with lactose-free or lactose-reduced milk, smaller amounts of milk more frequently, aged cheeses such as swiss and cheddar (which contain less lactose), and yogurt containing active bacterial cultures. However, a systematic review found these interventions were no more beneficial than placebo in patients older than 4 years.

Consuming milk containing only A2 β-casein compared to both A1 and A2 β-casein reduced bloating, abdominal pain, stool frequency, and improved stool consistency in a cross-over study of 600 lactose tolerant and intolerant Chinese subjects.

In an RCT of lactose malabsorbers, combined administration of freeze-dried yogurt cultures and acid lactase increased lactose digestion, based on breath tests, and reduced symptoms more than either product alone.

In a 4-week cross-over trial, administration of DDS-1 strain of Lactobacillus acidophilus improved symptoms of diarrhea, abdominal cramping, and vomiting in response to a lactose challenge over placebo.
Educate patients about reading food labels to avoid products that contain lactose. See for hidden sources of lactose in the diet and recommended substitutions.

With dairy restriction, calcium levels can fall which can affect bone health, especially bone development in children. Consider recommending high-calcium foods or fortified calcium products such as cereal or orange juice. Supplementation with calcium may be necessary.
Individuals learn about their lactose tolerance by trial and error. Long-term dietary management balances lactose intake with acceptable GI symptoms.

An ultra-purified, high-concentration galacto-oligosaccharide (currently called RP-G28) is being developed for treatment of lactose intolerance. Early studies show significant reduction in symptoms, alteration in fecal microbiome, and improved milk/dairy consumption.
Symptoms are not thought to damage the GI tract and no known impact on mortality is attributed to LI, although prospective cohort studies are lacking.
There is no clear relationship between LI and colorectal cancer, although high dairy intake in populations with a low prevalence of LI may be protective.
A large prospective cohort study in Finland found no difference in growth or development among children.
There is no association between lactase persistent LCT-13910 C/T genotype and all-cause or cause-specific mortality based on a Danish general population study.
Life-long dietary management is thought to continue to control symptoms, although long-term follow-up studies are lacking.
In an Israeli follow-up study of 154 children with gastrointestinal symptoms and positive lactose hydrogen breath, most children (62.3%) were still observing a restricted diet.
Prevalence increases with age.
Evaluate diet for calcium and vitamin D intake. Consider supplementing accordingly to prevent osteoporosis.
LI is uncommon before 2 to 3 years of age.
By age 14 years, 54% of African Americans develop LI compared to 11% to 33% of Caucasian Americans.
Lactose-free and lactose-reduced milks are available through the Women, Infants and Children Nutritional Program.
Add adequate calcium supplementation as needed.

list.listitem: Milk, yogurt, ice cream, coffee creamer, cheese, sherbet, pudding, custard, and cream
Cottage cheese, cream cheese, butter, margarine, some yogurt, and aged cheese like swiss and cheddar
Lactose-free milk, enzyme supplement to milk, soy milk, soy-based yogurt. Use lactose-free milk for all your cooking and baking needs

Ingredients derived from milk contain lactose and should be avoided. These include whey, milk byproducts, curds, fat-free dry milk powder, malted milk, buttermilk, dry milk solids, cream, butter, cheese, and casein
Nonprescription and prescription medications, soft drinks

tr.td: Processed meat, lunch meat, and breaded meat
Canned salmon and sardines with edible bones, shrimp, oysters, and tofu
Baked goods, pancake and bread mixes, instant cereal, breakfast cereals and bars
Creamed soups, vegetables, or sauces; instant potatoes or soup
Broccoli, Bok Choy, greens, spinach, and dried beans and peas
Ranch or cheese topping on snacks, packaged mixes, chocolate
Almonds, Brazil nuts, sunflower seeds, and black molasses
Instant tea or coffee, powdered hot chocolate, milk-based nutritional supplements
Calcium-fortified orange juice or soy milk
